title: Structural stability: compare the relationship before and after a known date
concepts: economic reading of a regime change

explain.prompt: In 5–7 sentences: how did the Brent–WTI relationship change on 1 January 2016 (spread level, spread volatility, short-run pass-through)? Each sub-period is strongly cointegrated, yet the full 2012–2019 sample is not (Engle-Granger p ≈ 0.28): why? What would you have concluded from the full sample alone? Why must the break date come from outside the data, and what do the placebo dates show?
rubric: Before 2016 the WTI discount averaged ≈ 0.17 log points (≈ 16 %), after ≈ 0.06 (≈ 6 %); the spread is less volatile after; the daily pass-through rises from ≈ 0.59 to ≈ 0.89 and the return correlation from ≈ 0.79 to ≈ 0.88.

Economic reading: with the export ban WTI was landlocked and partly priced off local US balances; once exports were allowed the arbitrage tied it to Brent — a smaller discount and a closer daily link.

Each regime is cointegrated (EG p ≈ 0), but one regression over 2012–2019 forces a single equilibrium; its residual inherits a level shift of ≈ 0.11 in 2016 and looks non-stationary, so Engle-Granger fails to reject (p ≈ 0.28) — a break distorts cointegration tests just as it distorts ADF.
From the full sample alone one would wrongly conclude 'no long-run relationship'.

The date comes from an identifiable event (end of the export ban) chosen before looking at the data; picking it by scanning for the largest change would invalidate standard inference. Placebo dates inside a regime (2014, 2018) show similar statistics on both sides.
Consequence: estimate the current relationship on the current regime and keep re-testing it on recent data.
